doc.title: Wilson "Chembo" Corniel interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, November 15, 2019

title: Learning jazz and other genres authentically, and non-Latin players' shallow Latin
summary: Latin players study jazz traditions properly, fitting in first; American club-date players often play Latin tunes wrongly.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: with the Latin people there, we go out of our way to learn jazz traditionally. You know we go and spend the time so when we’ve got to set up and do a jazz gig it’s going to sound like a jazz gig. It’s not going to sound like a watered down fake chords, you’re gonna know the theory behind what you’re doing and stuff, so you can go out and play authentically. You’re not going to wash it down. You know each style of music — if I’m going to study flamenco music it’s going to be the traditional style. If I’m going to do some straight ahead jazz, if I’m going to do some pop music, you know there’s certain elements — I won’t play the same with each genre. There’s a key — I call it the law — the law is there’s certain laws — I can’t do this here, I don’t need a full Latin set up when I do a pop gig. So this is why I have my drums and my effects, my toys, because this is more colors. I do a Latin gig and I know I’m expecting conga, bongo, timbales. If I’m going to do a jazz gig, you know, it’s a different approach of playing that, even as a percussionist. So I’m not playing the same thing, banging away to everything. There’s a certain elements. See I play with Grady Tate and he’s a singer, and lightly. I don’t even have to put my hand on the conga, the full hand on it. I just do my fingertips just to get a little sound, enough to back him up without overpowering him. And Latin music, you’ve got to blow. So you’ve got to know those things first. So when I sit down here and the guy says, “Man you sound great” but I haven’t done anything. All I did was follow the path that I was supposed to. And then on top of that you put your own soul into it.
In other words you fit in first.

Right. First. And then you’ve got to experiment. Like you go through the doors, see what’s happening in there, you know you can walk through further, say hi, so you’re kind of introducing yourself to each song and each style. So this is why we have — we also, you know we go out into studying this full, to the full extent of each genre. Latin people. So and it dawns on me why not, when the American people play a Latin tune, they won’t go out and study these laws — the basics — a little tumbao on the piano, a little montuno. How to play, we told — the same situation. I’m doing a lot of club dates so the guy wanted to play a little mambo, dance music you know, salsa, right? The piano player goes [scats]. I said, “What is that?” “That’s Brazil, that’s a samba.” [scats] It’s not 1-4-5 montuno as a Latin thing. So that’s all they have in their mind because they don’t take the time out to study Noro Morales, Tito Puente, Machito, you know the basic things. You know we had Ray Santos who just passed away teaching at City College and teaching these young students the way to do a certain — and it’s easy but they don’t take the time out into studying our music in order for that to sound correct at a club date.
